items.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022
items.q: I had Gene Perla the bass player, adjust them... Gene Perla, the bass player, did that. He and his friend. And they did it with half a dozen, six, seven, eight of my play-a-longs.

ctx.x: There’s — it’s an interesting thing to have to do.

Yeah, it is. And with some of the piano players I would say you can mix it up you know. Sometimes use like two hands but a little further apart, but then don’t stay like that because you’ve got your solo stuff here in the higher register. Bring them back more into the middle. And another thing I would have to say too is after we’d get into the fourth or fifth minute of something and it’s starting to cook, I mean it really is feeling good, watch it — piano player, don’t get to soloing. Pull back please, relax. And…
And you had the foresight to put on tuning notes. Correct?

items.title: Aebersold Jamey — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: we have been able to digitally have Gene Perla, the bass player, up in Easton, Pennsylvania, with his program that he’s got... It’s fantastic.

ctx.x: There you’ve got Volume 6 with Charlie Parker, and then Miles Davis, Sonny Rollins and Woody Shaw.

Incidentally, the Volume 1, the Volume 3, the Volume 6... Volume 14—Benny Golson. Volume 17—Horace Silver. Volume 18—Horace Silver. We, as of the last year or two...we have slowed those records down, those Play-A-Longs, and now they have two CDs— slower tempos and original tempos. Because jazz education has moved through the years down and down age-wise, so you’ve got 10-, 11- and 12-, 13-year-old people trying to play Volume 1, our Charlie Parker tunes, our Horace Silver tunes. So we’ve been able to digitally…
And was it pitch control...not pitch control...
